Vigilius's Latin is highly mannered and in places obscure; several renderings are tentative. Letter 1: 'suggerere' is taken as 'set forth'. 'impensis pusillae fidei votis' is uncertain. The clause 'cujus minister ... praecesserit' lacks a connective and looks defective; '[since]' is supplied. In section II, the subject of 'Verum ille, subductus ...' is unclear: it may be a child saved from death, and the passage may be corrupt. 'haud umquam impiger' would literally say 'never diligent', which contradicts the context; 'never sluggish' is the assumed sense. The sentence 'Denegare non potui ...' is abrupt and its sense uncertain. 'cum eodem' carries a footnote mark in the edition; '[love]' is inferred. Letter 2: 'Comitivam ... comitibus' is a pun on comes, 'companion' and an office-holder. 'quod semper debere ... expendi feceram' is obscure and possibly corrupt. 'Anagnia' is the form printed here for the Anaunian district (Val di Non). 'inquilinum' is doubtful: it may mean a settled or local name. The sentences 'Positus namque ...' and 'Nam praetermissis ...' do not construe fully; the second apparently breaks off. In the first, 'exhibet' has no clear subject beyond 'locus'. 'occiderent' could mean 'should fall' or 'should kill'; 'fall' is preferred. Parenthesised words in section III, (fidei) and (violatae), are given as the edition marks them.

The Latin is highly mannered and in places obscure or probably corrupt. IV: 'praedone' is read as 'a praedone' (from the robber). The closing sentence ('nisi quia impossibilem me...') is elliptical, and the rendering is tentative. V: 'emerita' is taken with 'quiete'. VI: the Africans who arm themselves for a voluntary death are probably the Donatist circumcellions, though the text does not name them. The sentence on withdrawal ('unde vana similisque timori est secessisse, religio') is uncertain. VII: 'timor, non timuit' is taken as 'an object of fear'. 'Luci' is taken as genitive of 'lucus' (grove), apparently with wordplay on 'lux' (light) and life. 'Sumus a gentibus increpat' cannot stand as printed: a passive such as 'increpiti' is assumed. VIII: 'index' (rendered 'indicator') is punned on throughout, and seems to suggest the bellwether as well as one who points out or testifies. The quotation 'Et index meus in matutino' appears to be Ps. 72(73):14 in an Old Latin form. 'Aerii testis' is obscure: taken literally as 'airy witness', but it may conceal a bronze object (aerea testa?) or a corruption. 'Seductor salutis' is odd and is rendered literally. 'Septima repromissionis sorte' is unexplained.

IX: 'horti facient' read as 'horti faciem'; the sense of the final clause is uncertain. 'virge' read as 'virgo'. 'Isidis amenda' is probably 'amandatio' or similar (banishment); uncertain. The reference to the sixth weekday holding 'a part of the Lord's body' is obscure.

nodes.text: THE TWO LETTERS OF SAINT VIGILIUS.
(From Gallandi's Bibliotheca, vol. VIII, pp. 203-206.)
FIRST LETTER.
TO SIMPLICIAN, BISHOP OF MILAN.
On the martyrdom of Saints Sisinnius, Martyrius and Alexander.
I. To the holy lord and venerable Father Simplician, to be preferred above all good men, Vigilius, bishop of the Church of Trent, [sends] greeting.

Although, when mention is made of Martyrs, merits are not commended by words but words by merits, and it would rather befit constancy to pass over in silence those whose virtue has been proved, yet because piety has urged, debt has admonished and duty has compelled me to set forth the causes, places and battles of the martyrdom, I have not denied my tongue, trembling with grief, to the page, since neither could a lamp be hidden under a bushel, nor the voice of holy blood be kept silent. For after many steps of patience and diligent battles, a fresh iniquity of faithlessness has come upon us: ministers in churches that had recently been founded were provoked, and they won the titles of martyrdom; ready for all things, gladly bearing all things, giving occasion to no one, they earned glory by the occasion of glory. Their life, that I may relate the highest peaks of the matter for the sake of making it known, was singular both in its care and in its purpose: for all of them, free of the bond of marriage, offered to God spotless souls as holy victims. Now the first, Sisinnius by name, brought the new peace of the Christian name to a barbarian nation; this peace he constantly guarded through a series of years, as far as lay in him, acknowledging no fellowship in polluted hospitality, and, like Lot in Sodom, he kept his religion with astonishing fear. But a safe sheep, though set in the midst of wolves, he sought a fold, which, generous in spending on the vows of a tiny faith, he was the first to found in that region. Of this [fold] he deserved, if you will deign to review it with me, to be the minister as though by debt, [since] as an old man he went before [the others] in merit as in age.

II. The lector Martyrius too, joined to him as a support, with the pledge of his very name already commending him, took on as a catechumen the beginnings of religious profession after temporal military service. For having thrown away his belt and rejected the company of his parents and of his brothers according to the flesh, understanding that he had obtained grace from God, the author of true light, and joined by office among the lectors, he was the first to sound the song of divine praise in the ears of the deaf region, ever attentive to spiritual works, wearied by continual fasts, the tutor of his own reading, anxious for the winning of souls. Wherefore in a brief outlay of time he sent on ahead so great an interest that the crown was deservedly entrusted to him. Why should I relate the souls set free, gone forth in full light to the bosom of Abraham, whom the treacherous observance of superstitious days, the law of nature being set aside, was condemning to a cruel death? But that one, withdrawn from his mother's breasts swollen with milk and nourished in a foreign place, was always seeking the affection fitting for a mother, about to declare to seeing eyes the resurrection preached by examples. These are a few things out of many.

III. Alexander too, brother of Martyrius by blood, as the third completing the victim of the trinity, unlocked an equal door of confession. For as a stranger for God's sake he left his homeland and parents, a faithful companion in trials, great-souled in faith, inclined to mercy. And if my testimony is at all believed, they are not to be ranked one above another, except each by the other; and there was no need for them to be commended, except perhaps because it was fitting. But so far your weariness has been relieved, if you still willingly admit [this] to your ears. For the smoky heathenry grew hot against the warmth of faith, through the devil's zeal, with the flame of fury, thereafter creeping on as a slow tinder, because with means, as I said, devoted from the poverty of faith, the deacon had been the first to set up in that place the tabernacle of a church. There was added also to the titles of a just cause that, by the faithful ministry of a deacon, he forbade victims to be given over to the devil from a Christian house, and wished the banner of the passion to be carried before the banner of the deadly lustration. For a band, summoned under one reward, flew together to blood; and in the morning hours, finding him greatly worn out by the wounds of the previous day, and seized in his bed in no other state, it buried him in a well-earned rest. The lector too, never sluggish, was serving also at the pre-dawn ministry, the lector whom the deacon attended in the sacrifice; and the aforementioned Martyrius was supplying medicine for the wounds, which they completed by the work in which they were seized. For the lector, withdrawing to the garden which adjoined the church, was captured, and planted the tree of his life from the root. The door-keeper too was joined to the passion: seized in his lodging, as he did not offer his soul, so he did not refuse it. But all, gathered into one, dragged over some distance, breathed out their souls to God. And the bodies of two were led along lifeless; but for the third, the more tenacious his life, the more keenly felt was his punishment: for alive he watched his own funeral. A pyre was prepared from the sacred roofs or beams of the church: this flame veiled the martyrs. With a reverent vow we are considering among ourselves that a basilica be built in that place where they first earned the testimony of glorious faith. Now console me, unworthy, a sharer in both, with fatherly love, and with the same [love] approach the saints themselves as an intercessor, so that on that day, all things now laid aside, I, a sinner, may touch the hem either of the priests or of the martyrs. We greet your holiness with special service: I beg that you may deign to commend my grief to the Lord. Likewise in another hand. I could not refuse what was yours in us; it would become more glorious by the merit of the one receiving, not by the favour of the one bestowing. Now the day of the saints' passion was the fourth [day] before the Kalends of June, the sixth day of the week, at the break of light.
LETTER II.
TO SAINT JOHN CHRYSOSTOM.

On the same martyrs. Here begins the letter of Saint Vigilius on the praises of the most blessed martyrs Sisinnius, Alexander and Martyrius, whose relics reached John, bishop of the city of Constantinople, through Jacobus, an illustrious man.

I. A new guest of charity would not approach holy ears, nor, unprovoked, press upon the modesty of a first move, nor would one unknown begin an address, unless a reward also provoked him. And so, dearest brother, the course and fullness of the present letter will begin from an apostolic man, so that by an easy transition you may understand that the praises of the martyrs follow. For Jacobus, a man faithful in heavenly desires, intending to lay down his dignity of *comes* [a court office, literally companion] among the companions of Christ, asked for the relics of the recent saints, still smoking with vapour. I said 'lay down', because a dignity that is heaped up with the Lord cannot be put away. To him I, being quite fearful and not unaware of the matter, having wrestled with myself over the disposal [of the relics], and being the less fit as a distributor, almost refused out of fear: what I had always caused to be paid out as owed, so that one might gain interest. I confess: I greatly feared, with a private fear, the private loss of many, had I not looked to Jacobus, who would hand [them] over to holy John as a kind of nourishment of reverence, so that, love being delegated through the religious names of the martyrs, a brotherhood not foreign might be brought and joined once more by blood. Gladly accepting among other things this reputation of faith too, which smiled well upon my grief, I only delayed, I did not refuse. I delayed, so that my slowness might again be openly shown, I who had not at all deserved to follow my companions. I confess, I wished it: but the crown of righteousness does not lie in desire alone. But now, if a fitting order will not be burdensome to thirsting ears, I will begin from the situation of the region and of the road, following the chief traces of events without tedium, so that the flood of merits may flow together more readily, if with capacious love you reach the origin of the spring.

II. For the place (whose resident name is Anagnia), situated twenty-five stades from the city, shut in by narrow jaws as much by faithlessness as by nature, opened by almost a single approach (you might call it the road of the three martyrs), which, lying back on a gentle slope, with a valley sinking on every side, with forts set all round in a crown, its neighbours conspiring together in faithlessness, displays a sort of spectacle, a stage of nature. The place lacked a cause: but Christ was a fit cause, so that the devil's show might give a procession to martyrdom. Let the account of the places not be hateful to the ears of the listener. For the place, hollow among the mountains and echoing, was always a bad companion to itself: when the soldiery of Christ first climbed up to it, the savage heathenry, often roused by trumpets, was inflamed with rival fury and the blasts of war. But one kind of the saints' fighting was perfect: to bear all things, when provoked to yield, to endure patiently, as men who were to suffer to restrain public fury by private gentleness, to conquer by declining [battle]. But predestined glory pressed them hard with the titles of a ripe end, which the due order had brought forth. For, passing over digressions and cutting off the long windings (only I will not keep silent) by which the virtue of the martyrs was nourished, with a brevity that will take away the loss of praise.

III. When the name of the Lord was still foreign in the aforesaid region, and there was no sign to show the seal of (faith), there were these men, then singular in number, now in merit, strangers as much in religion as in race, by whom God, being unknown, was not undeservedly preached, settled by a quiet way of life over a long time, while no benefit to the faith stirred [them]. But now, if the cause of the hatred rising against the Lord is sought, the charge was (violated) peace; because one of them, Sisinnius by name, older than the other two, in whom even old age alone would be venerable, raised up a church at his own expense. Richer in faith than in means, wealthy in spirit, poor in property, he handed over the fold to the shepherd. He became the watchman of what he had founded: but the fold was hateful to the wolves. The devil's ruin envied the raised roof. This was the first lot of martyrdom, that sheep, while they pursue the lamb, should fall. There was added, like a victim, that cause more just before God: that when they desired to lead the evil lustration around the boundaries of the fields in a deadly pageant, and were both trampling and defiling the sprouting crops, about to tread underfoot Christ's shoots too, crowned with mournful ornaments, with the devil's howled chant, with processions of various beasts, with banners raised against the Lord's house, they were compelling a man lately converted from their own people to give victims to the works of darkness. When the Lord's ministers could scarcely see this done without guilt of their own, since by standing by they too seemed to share in the confused works, on that day the bodies of the saints were pledged to deadly slaughter, though the palm of victory was deferred.

IV. Here, brother, I wish to compare with you for a little the titles of these events, so that no one may think this martyrdom pedestrian, undertaken in humility: for every good that is present is thought cheap; whereas it is new and marvellous, raised up without the envy of time, and so completed that nothing went before it and nothing follows; rather it is unique, being alone closed by the consummation granted to it. Because he guards the sheep from the robber, he is shown, I think, to be no hireling but a disciple of Christ; and he who flees is a hired man; he who does not desert is a shepherd. He who lays down his life lives; he who keeps it loses it. For what else did the Master and Lord do, except not to abandon deserters; or the Lamb, except to defend the ewe-lamb, so that he might be consummated as a holy victim for the sheep? But as I am about to enter the gate of the passions, having set out their manifold cause, I will not draw in foreign praise, nor will I steal: for it is not for martyrs to want what belongs to others, nor for priests to deceive; except that I confess myself incapable, in pursuing these things as in relating them, and in this least of all, since I will say less [than the truth].

V. For after the banner of the devilish lustrations, which, as we have related, was a sign of the glory soon to come, the ascent is made to the crown, deferred by one night. For in the morning hours of dawn, as the shadow of the sky suddenly gave way, an unexpected but conspiring band gathered, armed with stakes hardened in the fire and with axes, and with whatever the devil's anger had made a weapon for those who searched; and there, some levites being caught in the church singing the morning hymn, a vast devastation takes place, a savage plundering: all things are profaned, the secret as well as the divine mysteries; religion, finally, becomes plunder. Let no one think this was a common contest, when either insensible idols are torn down by sensible men, or masses of stones are moved along with their builders, so that of the worshipper and the thing to be worshipped you would be unsure which to judge the harder. Christ the Rock was being harassed in all of them, the corner-stone was being rejected by the heathen, to be proved again, and to build up with pure blood a ruin that was rising. Among these things faith had its own spectacle. The body of Sisinnius, then a deacon, was confined to a bed, pierced and wounded also with earlier wounds, from when he was ordered either to call back a sheep to the sacrifice or to become a sacrifice himself, unless he consented to the deadly offerings; struck with the trumpet on which they sounded the devil's chant, not undeservedly, he who had been the first to bring in the sound of faith; cut down with axes, he who was defending the unfruitful tree of heathenry from the axe. And so as not to draw out further what is established: he is caught, as we have said, in the well-earned rest of his bed; he confessed, I believe, so that by a private mystery he might come more quickly to the cross, to set free the paralytic people.

VI. Martyrius too, the reader, is bound with ropes across a beam: a confessor in like manner and a champion of his own name, who first then, and now alone, had sung a new song in a foreign land, amid the noisy and rough shouts of the herdsmen, having already at that time rendered to God praises of sweet speech, as I recalled above; and he had brought medicine or poultices to the deacon Sisinnius, to heal his pains, though he was to receive wounds himself, calling back with choice draughts the fleeing soul, not for the body, but for the passion. But the saint, the road of martyrdom to Christ being now determined, refused the drink of water, because the wine of the passion had come, which he had mixed from the streams of the truer life in the cup held out to him. So, caught in this care, he who was always concerned for the holiness of souls, not born for himself alone, nor surely to live for himself alone, withdrew into the seclusion of the garden that adjoined [the church]; that is, he did not withdraw from the church. For the church, as you know better, is a garden, planted with hedges of living commandments. He did not thrust forward his body, which he had no wish to deny; nor did he take up the boldness of rashness through confidence in his piety, as is said of those in the regions of Africa who arm themselves for a voluntary death: what they do without fear, they court from swollen pride. But the future martyr stood, captured, free; undaunted, having confessed; giving thanks, wounded; hurt in body, secure in mind, his head cut, washed in blood in a private baptism. No one deserved to follow him who was thought to be fleeing; hence his having withdrawn is an empty scruple and like fear: but the just confession of the captured man showed that the one stood only in order to conquer, and the other withdrew so that the persecutor too might perish in his glory. From the garden to which he had fled, Martyrius is brought. This withdrawal is a kind of mystery: that as a purple flower, a dweller in springtime places, a rose might deservedly be dyed, going before as a new martyr; or among the white tresses of the lilies, all watered through baptism and planted by a death that returns to life, the will for life might silently be declared. Pierced also with stakes, he was led to the idol: but he merited to be a victim before he reached the devil's altar.

VII. The third crown of the Lord too, about to honour Alexander, is completed. He found access as one of the household, he who kept watch at the doors of Christ; with him as guard, the covered hearts of the heathen had torn the veil of the temple. Eagerly sought by the multitude, since he was well known to all for his zeal for the faith, he was captured, yet not made captive; an object of fear, he did not fear. The disciple of Christ was often mocked, and in this a greater labour in the martyrs' torments made the punishment more lively; and so, to make up for his rank by the excess of his suffering, he merited by lot that nothing among the three should be lesser. For with the others fury did not delay the torments; slow punishment kept this man for the Lord: he perceived that he knew what he was bearing, a spectator of his own body; and although the wounds inflicted had postponed the martyr who had been the deacon, mentioned above, the torments showed this man to be their own guardian. For when the bodies had been joined and tied together and dragged through the public way in the manner of dogs, though not to return to their vomit, Alexander was led alive among them with his feet bound in, to leave part of his quivering limbs along the rocks, until he was brought to the edge of the grove, of life, I mean. After this they went against the religious heights, that is, the lofty temples of God; after the bodies, the roofs were laid on the ground, a pyre was made from the sacred beams, in the sight of Saturn, an idol ancient with long ages. When the twin and brother bodies had first been sent into the fire, Alexander stood wounded, to confess again; to him the reward of life was offered, that he should lose his life: if he wished to escape the flame before him, let him say that he consented to their darkness. But to him, looking askance and rejecting the gifts of the impious, there was a light against the light before his eyes; fear of punishment prevented punishment; the heat of faith drove back the flame; the order of the passion too kept reverence for rank. He is received last: but he is not crowned lowest among the brothers. Fulfilled, brothers, in the three ministers, now indeed at the banquet of heavenly joy, is the mystery of the Trinity; since others too could have suffered as a living victim, by a like lot, were not all things judged perfect by the number three. For we were perhaps not the smallest part among these things: and on their account we are reproached by the heathen; nor did we abandon our companions: but rank has its choosing.

VIII. Many things besides, in the days as the passion drew near, were not so much displayed as painted by the truth, which we set aside for brevity, so that through these few deeds we may teach the mysteries more fully. If, however, you will deign patiently to read over with me what has been related, then from the very cradle, indeed, of the region: Sisinnius was a Cappadocian by race or a Greek, among you of the first blood in former times; swift in faith, great-souled in spirit, lavish of labour, persevering in all things, closing his course with a palm not late, destined to come in the seventh lot of the promise, joined always by the bond of charity, harmonious in peace, holding the reins of divine discipline, the tamer of so great a yoked people, Christ's indicator; lastly, holding the leadership of the way for the flock to come or for his brother blood (as use, the teacher of things, says), he is recognised as the bold trampler of danger and its pioneer, so that the columns may follow safely close behind. So in our morning indicator of the faith there was the primacy of blood and of leadership: who, after showing the way, led to life or brought in to glory, the one who led away to salvation, the knower of the truth; as the Prophet testifies: And my indicator in the morning. And so that the deeds might heap up the mysteries still more, and that its Indicator might not lack an indication, when they were dragging the lifeless body of holy Sisinnius like an animal, they tied to the neck of the airy witness a hollow ringing thing, which the common people call a bell; insulting the body, reproaching the dead, taunting that Christ was no avenger; and in mocking the Lord's disciple they fulfilled a saving mystery. For what did that ringing mean, or that sound useful to the animals that follow, fitting also for adornment, hung from the neck? Only that a voice might belch out the name of Christ, crying hoarsely to the deaf, and show him in all things to be the leader of the people as of a flock. For he first rang out the word of the religious voice, he first sounded through the hollow valleys: to creatures as yet almost brute beasts, or certainly to cattle, a leader to untouched pasture, a ringer of a new hearing, a chewer of the flowering law among the heathen.

IX. In the order set forth, Martyrius, following up also the name that was his, fulfilled the prophecy that he held: he set forth the parable of his name, a true revealer in all things: he smiled on the name by which he was called, and heaped it up with merits: he established his birth-name, that as by origin, so by passion it should come to pass. Why should I unfold the secrets of the garden, accomplice of his punishment? That he betook himself there first, to that which as a martyr he entered again, the gate of paradise, meditating on its pure delight and the venerable pleasures of its spring; about to plant in green places a living flower, still clinging badly to the thorn of the world; pointed out by a virgin, whose garden it was. Why do you turn me back again to the mysteries that took place? She betrayed him, a virgin who always wished to keep her own: she wished to let go the one she had received: she chose the cultivator whom she had approved. Already with the affection of a known love she held God too as one invited, as Solomon says in the Canticles, Let my brother come down into his garden (Cant. 5:1). He came down, and surely came down: for he would not go out whom a rich will had loved, also at the time of the passion, to express a thing known in our own times. In a garden, with the Jews, Iscariot seized the Lord. Let no one find fault with such a withdrawal of the disciple: so the Master and Lord is found. He was thought to be the gardener, the waterer of the living, the planter of souls. The garden, then, is the refuge not of one fleeing but of one taking refuge, and to those who understand, the garden's appearance has merited paradise.

X. But what could the mystery of death confer on Alexander, who fulfilled it all while living; except that his name smiled at the vice of the people, so that Anagnia might be thought an Alexandria, religious in private portents, full of demons, two-formed with Anubises, many-formed with idols, half-men, which is [a thing] for mockers of the law; full of Isis's banishment, Serapis's flight; finally the alluring mother of resident crimes, or rather stepmother; nursling of a brood of vipers, poisoned through the offspring of its race, which does not know how to be conceived unless it rejoices in the father's bereavement; does not know how to grow unless it is born by death; does not know how to live unless it has not known its mother; so that in the conversion to faith the offspring of an evil brood, conceived at the loss of God the Father, born with its head denied, brought forth through the pierced womb of mother Church, might take the origin of life through the death of the saints; but now it grows more fruitful by loss, more lively by death, more joyful after grief. For it is plain and fully perceived, what has been disclosed as the Scriptures dictate (Rom. 11:32), that all things were shut up under one sin, so that all might merit mercy. These are the hundredfold returns of the passion, by which that people now absolves its own guilt: captivity made them free, indulgence loosed the bound. The sky then consented to darkness, the light shuddered at the passion, confounded, I believe, by the blindness of a faithless mind.

XI. Believe, brother, the eyes of a brother. A certain shadow of black cloud covered, or rather overspread, the whole region; thunderbolts crashed close to the earth; a dreadful crash often thundered; flashing red fire shot forth more and more: you would have said the sky was an accomplice of the blood. After the shadow of a strange night, so to speak, it is no longer possible to hide a manifest truth under a mist. The day too betrayed the horror of the passion, not only shrinking back but bereaved. For the kindly light of the sixth weekday had come forth, ever after God a friend to martyrs: reverently holding still a part of the Lord's body, through its holy nurslings it rendered service to the servants of God, though envy vied with religion's lot to come. So the Lord asserts himself by his works; so he shows himself a companion in all things, that he is joined by equality and by time. I was a spectator, I confess, amid these mysteries, and a watcher at the ashes of the saints: I who did not merit to be a sharer felt that which I could not attain. I saw, scarcely believing myself even today: the deeds exceed the reverence of words reported: hence it will be God's part, brother, to affirm what he chose, and to bear witness for the witness. Receive now, brother, the gifts of the three youths, or three youths from the furnace, still almost walking amid the burning of panting fire; and had not the envious fury of the flame taken them up half-dead, the example of the history would have come to life again: so nearly with like honour did all things paint themselves: Voice, Dew, Number, Furnace. The Voice, a harmonious faith; the Dew, rain; the Furnace, the pyre; the Number, the Trinity.
